cheby/binary_trees.name: Cheby
cheby/binary_trees.notes: fmt form checked by hand: `cheby fmt` does not exist before M5. Rerun `cheby fmt` once it lands.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/binary_trees.name: Gleam
gleam/binary_trees.notes: type Tree { Empty Node(left, right) }; the loops are tail-recursive functions; 2^k is int.bitwise_shift_left. Every node, leaves included, is a fresh heap tuple: make takes the empty child as an argument and is pub (so Tree is pub too), because the Erlang compiler folds a leaf written as Node(Empty, Empty), or built from an Empty passed between private functions, into one shared literal (the same fix in Erlang and Elixir; OCaml uses Sys.opaque_identity).

zig/binary_trees.name: Zig
zig/binary_trees.notes: Tree nodes are allocated from std.heap.smp_allocator, as the SPEC requires for Zig. The other Zig programs use init.gpa, which on macOS is std.heap.c_allocator (libc malloc), because Zig always links libSystem there. Rust and C++ binary_trees use libc malloc, so this is the one benchmark where Zig's allocator differs from theirs.

odin/binary_trees.name: Odin
odin/binary_trees.notes: new(Node) from the default context.allocator (libc heap), one allocation per node, freed recursively after each check. No arena. On Unix the default heap allocator wraps calloc and adds an alignment header to every request (alignment - 1 + size_of(rawptr) bytes), so each 16-byte node becomes a zeroed allocation of about 32 bytes; this explains the RSS and time gap to Rust and C++.

erlang/binary_trees.name: Erlang
erlang/binary_trees.notes: Nodes are {node, L, R} with the atom nil for an empty child, as the SPEC prescribes. Every node, leaves included, is a fresh heap tuple: make/2 takes the empty child as an argument and is exported, because the compiler folds a leaf written as {node, nil, nil}, or built from a nil passed between local functions, into one shared literal (the same fix in Elixir and Gleam; OCaml uses Sys.opaque_identity).

elixir/binary_trees.name: Elixir
elixir/binary_trees.notes: Nodes are {:node, left, right} tuples with nil for absent; the loops are tail-recursive functions. Every node, leaves included, is a fresh heap tuple: make/2 takes the empty child as an argument and is public, because the compiler folds a leaf written as {:node, nil, nil}, or built from a nil passed between private functions, into one shared literal (the same fix in Erlang and Gleam; OCaml uses Sys.opaque_identity).

clojure/binary_trees.name: Clojure
clojure/binary_trees.notes: deftype Node [left right] with nil for absent; the loops are loop/recur.

koka/binary_trees.name: Koka
koka/binary_trees.notes: type tree { Empty; Node(left, right) }, one heap node per Node, freed by Perceus reference counting. Loops are tail-recursive functions. Nodes come from Koka's bundled mimalloc, its default allocator (Rust, C++ and Swift use the macOS libmalloc), and check frees each node as it walks it (Perceus) instead of in a separate destructor pass; both explain why Koka is ahead of Rust and C++ here.

ocaml/binary_trees.name: OCaml
ocaml/binary_trees.notes: type tree = Empty | Node of tree * tree. Every node, leaves included, is a fresh heap block: leaves are built from Sys.opaque_identity Empty, because ocamlopt makes Node (Empty, Empty) one shared static constant (the BEAM languages export their make function for the same reason).

cheby/nbody.name: Cheby
cheby/nbody.notes: fmt form checked by hand: `cheby fmt` does not exist before M5. Rerun `cheby fmt` once it lands.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/nbody.name: Gleam
gleam/nbody.notes: Bodies are a 7-field record in a list, rebuilt every step: the first body is folded against each later one, then the updated rest recurses (the SPEC recursive shape). sqrt is math:sqrt through @external, since gleam/float square_root is math:pow(x, 0.5) and not guaranteed correctly rounded. Gleam constants cannot hold arithmetic, so SOLAR_MASS is a function computing 4.0 * PI * PI; gleam format drops trailing zeros of the float literals (same binary64). About 50% slower than erlang/main.erl on the same shape, mostly because list.map and list.reverse are remote calls, where Erlang uses a local list comprehension and lists:reverse (the same BEAM cost explains Elixir's gap). The idiomatic gleam/list calls are kept on purpose.

go/nbody.name: Go
go/nbody.notes: Mutable Body structs in a slice, updated through pointers. Go's default arm64 FMA contraction is left on, which the SPEC allows.

erlang/nbody.name: Erlang
erlang/nbody.notes: Bodies are 7-tuples in a list, rebuilt every step: the first body is folded against each later one, then the updated rest recurses (the SPEC's recursive shape).

typescript/nbody.name: TypeScript
typescript/nbody.notes: Bodies are plain objects typed by an interface, mutated in place in an array. A class with parameter properties was about 6x slower: tsc's ES2022 target emits class field declarations ([[Define]] semantics, useDefineForClassFields defaults to true), V8 initializes the fields to undefined, and the later float stores then generalize them to tagged fields that box every value. Math.round on |x| with the sign restored gives half away from zero.

elixir/nbody.name: Elixir
elixir/nbody.notes: Bodies are 7-tuples in a list, rebuilt every step: the first body is folded against each later one, then the updated rest recurses (the SPEC's recursive shape). About 40% slower than erlang/main.erl, whose hot path is otherwise the same expression for expression: Enum.map(&move/1) and Enum.reverse are remote calls, where Erlang uses a local list comprehension and lists:reverse. Making both local (checked on the decompiled beam) closes the gap; the idiomatic Enum calls are kept on purpose.

clojure/nbody.name: Clojure
clojure/nbody.notes: Bodies are a deftype with ^:unsynchronized-mutable ^double fields behind a definterface, in a vector, updated in place (the representation the SPEC allows for Clojure numeric code).

koka/nbody.name: Koka
koka/nbody.notes: Immutable struct body (7 float64 fields) in a list, rebuilt every step by matching `Body(x, y, z, vx, vy, vz, m)` and calling the constructor, so Perceus reuses unique records in place. Not the copy-update syntax `b(vx = ...)`: Koka 3.2 compiles it through optional arguments, boxing every float64 field, and allocates a fresh record (in review, 7.9 s at bench against 3.4 s for the constructor and 2.8 s for match-and-rebuild). Pair loop: the first body folded against the rest, then recurse. Default clang FMA contraction (allowed by the SPEC).

ocaml/nbody.name: OCaml
ocaml/nbody.notes: array of records with mutable float fields (a flat all-float record), updated in place

cheby/spectral_norm.name: Cheby
cheby/spectral_norm.notes: A(i, j) is written out in row_sum and column_sum instead of in an `entry(i, j) -> Float` helper. The helper is the more idiomatic shape, but a Float returned from a function is boxed (D-453), and the helper version measured about 1.65x slower at n = 1000 (2.04-2.13 s against 1.25-1.27 s), which would take the bench size (n = 5500) from about 60 s to about 100 s of user time, against the 300 s timeout. fmt form checked by hand: `cheby fmt` does not exist before M5. Rerun `cheby fmt` once it lands.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/spectral_norm.name: Gleam
gleam/spectral_norm.notes: Vectors are lists, walked with tail-recursive sums; A(i, j) is a helper function (Gleam cannot ask for inlining; writing the formula out in the loops measured only about 10% faster at n = 2000). sqrt is math:sqrt through @external, since gleam/float square_root is math:pow(x, 0.5).

go/spectral_norm.name: Go
go/spectral_norm.notes: Default build, which the SPEC allows. On arm64 the Go compiler fuses `x*y + z` into FMADDD by default (the Go spec permits fused multiply-add), so `sum += a(i, j) * xj` in timesA and timesAt becomes an fmadd on the loop-carried dependency, whose latency is longer than a plain fadd. Like the cpp row (clang's default -ffp-contract=on), this explains most of the gap to Rust and Zig, which emit separate fmul and fadd: about 1.3 s against about 0.85 s at the bench size. Writing `float64(a(i, j) * xj)` would stop the fusion, but the code is kept in its plain, default-contraction form because the SPEC does not require non-fused arithmetic here (unlike mandelbrot).

cpp/spectral_norm.name: C++
cpp/spectral_norm.notes: Default build, clang's default -ffp-contract=on, which the SPEC allows. clang fuses `sum += entry * x[j]` into an fmadd on the loop-carried dependency, whose latency is longer than a plain fadd: with -ffp-contract=off the same source ran about 25-35% faster (user 0.88-1.02 s vs 1.32 s) with the same output. Kept at the default because the SPEC does not require non-fused arithmetic here (unlike mandelbrot).

erlang/spectral_norm.name: Erlang
erlang/spectral_norm.notes: A(i, j) is a helper a/2 marked -compile({inline, [a/2]}), so erlc inlines it into the two inner loops (about 23% faster at n = 2000 than a plain call, which boxes the returned float). Vectors are lists, walked with tail-recursive sums.

typescript/spectral_norm.name: TypeScript
typescript/spectral_norm.notes: Float64Array vectors, preallocated output and scratch arrays reused across rounds. The matrix entry's denominator is computed with 32-bit integer ops (>>> 1 for the exact halving), as the benchmarks-game JavaScript entries do; plain / 2 in doubles gives the same value and was about 20% slower.

elixir/spectral_norm.name: Elixir
elixir/spectral_norm.notes: A(i, j) is a helper a/2 marked @compile {:inline, a: 2}, so it is inlined into the two inner loops. Vectors are lists, built with Enum.map over the index list and walked with tail-recursive sums.

clojure/spectral_norm.name: Clojure
clojure/spectral_norm.notes: Persistent vectors: mapv over the indices, reduce-kv over the input vector, A(i, j) a primitive ^long ^long -> ^double fn. Floats are boxed in the vectors and at each reduce-kv step.

koka/spectral_norm.name: Koka
koka/spectral_norm.notes: list<float64> vectors with the SPEC's sequential formulation: map over an index list built once, tail-recursive dot product per element. Integer (arbitrary-precision int) denominator.

ocaml/spectral_norm.name: OCaml
ocaml/spectral_norm.notes: float array with for loops; entry is a helper marked [@inline], since ocamlopt without flambda otherwise calls it and boxes its float result (2.1x slower)

nim/spectral_norm.name: Nim
nim/spectral_norm.notes: Default -d:release keeps Nim's overflow and bounds checks; the checked integer arithmetic in A(i, j) roughly doubles the run time against -d:danger (about 1.8 s vs 0.9 s at n = 5500), which is not used.

cheby/mandelbrot.name: Cheby
cheby/mandelbrot.notes: The loops are top-level tail-recursive functions, not the local `fn` loops the Cheby guide usually recommends: the current JIT boxes a Float on every local-function call (D-453), and a local-loop version measured 14.4 s at the bench size against 3.3 s. `cr` is computed inline in `walk` and the three totals are accumulator arguments, as in Erlang and Elixir: an earlier version with a `coordinate` helper (a non-tail call returning a Float, which the JIT boxes) and a new `Totals` record per point was about 15% slower. The result of float::from_int still costs 1 boxed Float per point. No `test` blocks, so the line count compares with the other implementations. fmt form checked by hand: `cheby fmt` does not exist before M5. Rerun `cheby fmt` once it lands.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/mandelbrot.name: Gleam
gleam/mandelbrot.notes: Three tail-recursive functions (rows, columns, escape_time); the totals are a small record; ci is computed inside the row loop.

go/mandelbrot.name: Go
go/mandelbrot.notes: Explicit float64(...) conversions on zr*zr, zi*zi and 2.0*zr*zi forbid Go's arm64 FMA fusion, as the SPEC requires.

odin/mandelbrot.name: Odin
odin/mandelbrot.notes: Odin does not contract a * b + c into FMA by default: the -o:speed binary has no fmadd/fmsub instructions (checked with otool).

elixir/mandelbrot.name: Elixir
elixir/mandelbrot.notes: The three loops are tail-recursive functions; float(N) is computed once and passed down, ci is computed inside the row loop so N = 0 never divides by zero.

clojure/mandelbrot.name: Clojure
clojure/mandelbrot.notes: Primitive double/long loop/recur locals; escape-time is a primitive ^double ^double -> ^long fn. The per-row totals come back from the column loop as a vector, once per row.

koka/mandelbrot.name: Koka
koka/mandelbrot.notes: No FMA (SPEC): koka_options passes -ffp-contract=off to clang. Loops are tail-recursive functions; the totals are a small struct.

ocaml/mandelbrot.name: OCaml
ocaml/mandelbrot.notes: while loop over float refs (unboxed); products bound with let before their sums so arm64 ocamlopt emits no fmadd (checked in the disassembly)

nim/mandelbrot.name: Nim
nim/mandelbrot.notes: -ffp-contract=off, as the SPEC requires for languages compiled through C

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/fannkuch_redux.name: Gleam
gleam/fannkuch_redux.notes: Rebuild shape on lists (gleam_stdlib has no indexed sequence): a flip is list.split + list.append(list.reverse(front), back), a rotation splits perm1 at r + 1. count is a list updated by index with small recursive helpers.

erlang/fannkuch_redux.name: Erlang
erlang/fannkuch_redux.notes: Rebuild shape on lists: a flip is lists:split + lists:reverse/2, a rotation splits perm1 at r + 1. count is a tuple updated with setelement.

swift/fannkuch_redux.name: Swift
swift/fannkuch_redux.notes: The flip is a plain swapAt loop over perm[0...k]. The library call perm[0...k].reverse() on an ArraySlice gave the same output but ran about 8 times slower at N = 10 under -O (1.27 s against 0.16 s), because swiftc 6.4 does not optimise the in-place slice reversal into a plain loop.

elixir/fannkuch_redux.name: Elixir
elixir/fannkuch_redux.notes: Rebuild shape on lists: a flip is Enum.split + Enum.reverse/2, a rotation splits perm1 at r + 1. count is a tuple updated with put_elem.

clojure/fannkuch_redux.name: Clojure
clojure/fannkuch_redux.notes: Index-update shape on persistent vectors (nth, assoc) for perm1 and count; no transients or Java arrays, per the SPEC.

koka/fannkuch_redux.name: Koka
koka/fannkuch_redux.notes: Index-update shape on vector<int>, through a value-returning `set` (a local var copy plus an index assignment): it copies when the vector is shared (the flip's first write, since the caller still holds perm1) and updates in place when it is unique (Koka's reuse of unique values). Loops are tail-recursive functions, as the SPEC says; the next permutation comes back as maybe<(perm1, count, r)>, one small allocation per permutation. An earlier version used while over local vars, whose captured vars became heap ref cells (about 20% slower).

cheby/word_freq.name: Cheby
cheby/word_freq.notes: fmt form checked by hand: `cheby fmt` does not exist before M5. Rerun `cheby fmt` once it lands.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/word_freq.name: Gleam
gleam/word_freq.notes: Two @externals, as the SPEC's Gleam guidance says: file:read_file/1 to read the file, and binary:split(Text, [<<" ">>, <<"\n">>], [global, trim_all]) to split it (gleam/string.split is grapheme-aware and far slower). Counting with dict.upsert in a gleam/dict, then list.sort with a comparator.

go/word_freq.name: Go
go/word_freq.notes: strings.FieldsSeq (the iterator form of strings.Fields, the same splitter) counts while splitting into map[string]int; keys are substrings of one string copy of the file. slices.SortFunc with cmp.Compare on counts and strings.Compare (byte order) on words.

zig/word_freq.name: Zig
zig/word_freq.notes: std.mem.tokenizeAny over the file buffer, std.StringHashMap(u64) with keys sliced from the buffer, std.mem.sort (stable).

odin/word_freq.name: Odin
odin/word_freq.notes: strings.fields_iterator (the iterator form of strings.fields) over the file buffer; map[string]int keyed by slices into the buffer; slice.sort_by.

cpp/word_freq.name: C++
cpp/word_freq.notes: File read into a std::string; a byte-scanning loop splits on space and newline; std::unordered_map<std::string_view, std::int64_t> keyed by views into the buffer; std::sort with a comparator.

java/word_freq.name: Java
java/word_freq.notes: Files.readString, String.split("\\s+") (skipping empty parts), HashMap<String, Integer> with merge, List.sort with a comparator using String.compareTo (ordinal). The regex split was chosen over the index loop with substring that the SPEC also allows; it builds the whole String[] first and, in a review measurement, cost roughly 2x the CPU of the index loop, so part of any JVM-vs-CLR gap here is the splitter (C# splits on chars, not a regex).

typescript/word_freq.name: TypeScript
typescript/word_freq.notes: readFileSync(path, "latin1"), text.split(/\s+/) skipping empty parts, Map<string, number>, Array.prototype.sort with a comparator that compares words with < (ordinal), not localeCompare.

swift/word_freq.name: Swift
swift/word_freq.notes: File read as Data into [UInt8]; split(whereSeparator:) on space and newline (builds the array of all word slices first, which the SPEC allows; this costs about 1 GB peak RSS at bench size); [String: Int] with the default hasher and subscript(_:default:); sorted(by:) with a String < comparator (Swift compares Strings by Unicode canonical ordering, which equals byte order for this ASCII input). The work is in a function: the same code as top-level main.swift code on globals ran about 7x slower.

csharp/word_freq.name: C#
csharp/word_freq.notes: File.ReadAllText, string.Split([' ', '\n'], RemoveEmptyEntries), Dictionary<string, int> (default ordinal comparer) updated with TryGetValue then the indexer (two lookups, the plain idiom its peers use), List.Sort with a comparator using string.CompareOrdinal

scala/word_freq.name: Scala
scala/word_freq.notes: Files.readString, String.split("\\s+") skipping empty parts, scala.collection.mutable.HashMap[String, Int] with getOrElse and update, Array.sortWith comparing words with < (ordinal String.compareTo). The regex split matches Java and is one of the two forms the SPEC allows; it builds the whole Array[String] first and costs more CPU than the index loop, so part of any JVM-vs-CLR gap here is the splitter (C# splits on chars, not a regex).

clojure/word_freq.name: Clojure
clojure/word_freq.notes: slurp, clojure.string/split on #"\s+" (leading empty part dropped), frequencies (a transient hash map), sort with a comparator: count descending, then compare on strings (String.compareTo, ordinal)

koka/word_freq.name: Koka
koka/word_freq.notes: Koka 3.2's std has no map, hash or sort: counts live in a hand-written persistent red-black tree keyed by string (FBIP zipper insert, after samples/basic/rbtree-fbip.kk), ordered by std cmp on strings (byte order), and the entries are sorted by a hand-written top-down merge sort. Splits with std split on "\n" then " ", skipping empty parts.

ocaml/word_freq.name: OCaml
ocaml/word_freq.notes: In_channel.input_all, String.split_on_char on '\n' then ' ' (empty parts skipped), the generic Hashtbl (find_opt then replace/add), List.sort with a comparator using String.compare (byte order).

nim/word_freq.name: Nim
nim/word_freq.notes: readFile, splitWhitespace, CountTable[string] (inc); entries copied to a seq and sorted with algorithm.sort and a comparator, not CountTable.sort.

ruby/word_freq.name: Ruby
ruby/word_freq.notes: String#split (whitespace), Enumerable#tally into a Hash, sort_by { [-count, word] }.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/json_roundtrip.name: Gleam
gleam/json_roundtrip.notes: gleam_json 3.x (over OTP's json module): json.parse_bits with gleam/dynamic/decode decoders into custom types, json.object (ordered) and json.to_string. The file is read with an @external to file:read_file/1.

go/json_roundtrip.name: Go
go/json_roundtrip.notes: Standard library encoding/json v1 with typed structs (json.Unmarshal / json.Marshal), no third-party module; output structs share tags, address and history with the parsed records.

zig/json_roundtrip.name: Zig
zig/json_roundtrip.notes: Standard library std.json with typed structs (parseFromSlice / Stringify.valueAlloc, minified by default), no third-party module; strings are slices into the input (alloc_if_needed, the default) and output structs share tags, address and history with the parsed records.

odin/json_roundtrip.name: Odin
odin/json_roundtrip.notes: core:encoding/json (standard library): json.unmarshal into structs, json.marshal with default options (compact). Each repetition's records, kept list and output are freed before the next.

cpp/json_roundtrip.name: C++
cpp/json_roundtrip.notes: nlohmann::ordered_json with NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_NON_INTRUSIVE structs: json::parse(text).get<std::vector<Record>>() and json(kept).dump(). Output records move tags/address/history out of the parsed records.

erlang/json_roundtrip.name: Erlang
erlang/json_roundtrip.notes: OTP json module (json:decode/1, json:encode/2). Output records, addresses and history entries are ordered key-value lists written through json:encode_key_value_list/2, because decoded maps encode in sorted key order.

java/json_roundtrip.name: Java
java/json_roundtrip.notes: Jackson 3 databind (tools.jackson), typed decoding into records; output records written in component order with writeValueAsBytes. jackson-core and jackson-annotations are databind's own dependencies. The deployable form is {build}/app: the class directory plus a copy of the three Jackson jars (about 2.5 MB), so artifact size counts them; like every Java row it excludes the JDK.

typescript/json_roundtrip.name: TypeScript
typescript/json_roundtrip.notes: Built-in JSON.parse and JSON.stringify (no library), interfaces for the records. Output records are new object literals in the SPEC's key order; address and history objects are shared with the parsed records, whose key order JSON.parse keeps. Counters are numbers (doubles), exact below 2^53; FNV-1a uses Math.imul and >>> 0.

swift/json_roundtrip.name: Swift
swift/json_roundtrip.notes: Foundation JSONDecoder into Decodable structs for parsing (no third-party library). Output by a small hand-written compact serializer (a JSONWritable protocol, objects written field by field in the SPEC's key order, strings escaped only when needed), as the SPEC allows: Swift 6.4's JSONEncoder writes keys in a different order on every run, and .sortedKeys would give alphabetical order. At bench size about 2.8 s of 3.3 s is JSONDecoder, about 0.35 s the serializer.

csharp/json_roundtrip.name: C#
csharp/json_roundtrip.notes: System.Text.Json from the base class library (no package): reflection-based JsonSerializer.Deserialize<List<Record>> into positional records and SerializeToUtf8Bytes of new output records, with JsonSerializerDefaults.Web for the camelCase keys. Output records share tags, address and history with the parsed records; records serialize in declaration order.

elixir/json_roundtrip.name: Elixir
elixir/json_roundtrip.notes: Built-in JSON module (JSON.decode!/1, JSON.encode!/1). Output records, addresses and history entries are structs with a derived JSON.Encoder, which writes keys in field order, because decoded maps encode in sorted key order.

scala/json_roundtrip.name: Scala
scala/json_roundtrip.notes: ujson (com.lihaoyi) value tree: ujson.read, a new ujson.Obj per kept record (insertion-ordered; address and history shared with the parsed tree, whose ujson.Obj keeps input key order), compact ujson.write

clojure/json_roundtrip.name: Clojure
clojure/json_roundtrip.notes: clojure.data.json read-str with :key-fn keyword and write-str (compact, default options). Output records are array-maps in the SPEC's key order; address and history entries are shared with the parsed records, which data.json builds as array-maps in input order (3 and 2 keys). Counters folded with reduce; the library is AOT-compiled once by setup (CLJ_AOT_LIBS) so the build compiles only main. The artifact size counts only the program's own classes ({build}/classes), not the data.json classes on the classpath, as Java counts its classes without Jackson.

koka/json_roundtrip.name: Koka
koka/json_roundtrip.notes: Koka has no JSON library: hand-written recursive-descent parser over a std sslice (next per character) into an ordered value tree (objects as key lists). Numbers follow the full JSON grammar: one without a fraction or exponent is an arbitrary-precision int (all of the data), any other is read from its text with std parse-float64 into a JFloat and written back with std show (plus ".0" when that shows no fraction), as a library would, and a serializer that conses string pieces in reverse and joins them once (reverse-join). Output records are new JObj values that share the parsed tags, address and history values, whose key order the tree keeps. output_bytes is `out.bytes.length`: std `string/bytes` is the string's own UTF-8 buffer in the C backend (`#1.bytes`, no copy), so it is an O(1) byte length.

ocaml/json_roundtrip.name: OCaml
ocaml/json_roundtrip.notes: Yojson.Safe.from_string into a value tree, decoded into typed records with Yojson.Safe.Util; output records built as `Assoc lists in key order and written with Yojson.Safe.to_string (compact).

nim/json_roundtrip.name: Nim
nim/json_roundtrip.notes: std/json: parseJson + to(seq[Record]) for typed decoding, % on the output objects (fields in declaration order) and $ for compact text. Most of the run time is std/json building a full JsonNode tree in both directions (parseJson before to(), % before $); the only streaming alternative in std, parsejson, is event-based parsing, which the SPEC forbids.

ruby/json_roundtrip.name: Ruby
ruby/json_roundtrip.notes: Standard library json (default gem 2.18.0, C extension; no third-party gem): JSON.parse into insertion-ordered Hashes and JSON.generate (compact). Output records are new Hashes built in the SPEC's key order, sharing tags, address and history with the parsed records.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/lru_cache.name: Gleam
gleam/lru_cache.notes: Shape C, as the SPEC's Gleam guidance says: gleam/dict for entries (key -> #(value, tick)) and by_tick (tick -> key), with an `oldest` counter for the evict. The checksum sorts the live (tick, key) pairs by tick. Loops are tail-recursive.

go/lru_cache.name: Go
go/lru_cache.notes: Shape B: map[int]*list.Element plus container/list with MoveToBack; an evict reuses the front element for the insert.

zig/lru_cache.name: Zig
zig/lru_cache.notes: Shape B: std.AutoHashMap(u64, u32) from key to slot plus an ArrayList of nodes linked by index; the map is rehashed once every `capacity` evictions, as the SPEC asks, because Zig's HashMap keeps tombstones and never rehashes at a constant size.

odin/lru_cache.name: Odin
odin/lru_cache.notes: Shape B: map[int]int from key to slot plus a [dynamic]Node doubly linked by index; map and node array reserve capacity up front.

cpp/lru_cache.name: C++
cpp/lru_cache.notes: Shape B: std::unordered_map<std::int64_t, std::list<Entry>::iterator> plus std::list<Entry>, splice to move a hit to the end; on eviction the front node is spliced to the back and overwritten (the SPEC's 'may reuse that node'), so a miss at capacity allocates no list node. The map reserves capacity up front.

erlang/lru_cache.name: Erlang
erlang/lru_cache.notes: Shape C: entries a map key -> {value, tick}, by_tick a gb_trees, evict with gb_trees:take_smallest, checksum with a gb_trees iterator. Most of the time goes to the persistent gb_trees delete and insert churn (about 2 us/op).

java/lru_cache.name: Java
java/lru_cache.notes: Shape A: LinkedHashMap<Long, Long>(capacity, 0.75f, true) in access order, get moves the key, removeEldestEntry evicts

typescript/lru_cache.name: TypeScript
typescript/lru_cache.notes: Shape B: Map<number, number> from key to slot plus an index-linked list in typed arrays (Int32Array prev/next, Float64Array keys/values); the evicted slot is reused. Numbers (doubles) throughout, exact below 2^47.

swift/lru_cache.name: Swift
swift/lru_cache.notes: Shape B: [Int: Int] from key to slot (default hasher, Dictionary(minimumCapacity:)) plus an array of Node structs linked by index; Int (64-bit) for the generator state and counters.

csharp/lru_cache.name: C#
csharp/lru_cache.notes: Shape B: Dictionary<long, LinkedListNode<(long Key, long Value)>> plus LinkedList<(long Key, long Value)> from System.Collections.Generic; a hit moves the node to the end with Remove and AddLast, an evict reuses the first node for the insert. The dictionary reserves capacity slots.

elixir/lru_cache.name: Elixir
elixir/lru_cache.notes: Shape C: entries a Map key -> {value, tick}, by_tick a :gb_trees, evict with :gb_trees.take_smallest, checksum with a :gb_trees iterator.

scala/lru_cache.name: Scala
scala/lru_cache.notes: Shape A: scala.collection.mutable.LinkedHashMap[Long, Long]; a hit is remove (the one lookup) then update, which moves the key to the end; evict head

clojure/lru_cache.name: Clojure
clojure/lru_cache.notes: Shape C as the SPEC prescribes for Clojure: entries a persistent hash-map key -> [value tick], by-tick a sorted-map tick -> key, evict with first; loop/recur, no LinkedHashMap interop. The row measures persistent-tree cost (shape C), not a mutable LinkedHashMap; no reflection or boxed-math warnings.

koka/lru_cache.name: Koka
koka/lru_cache.notes: Shape C: Koka 3.2's std has no map, so both maps (entries: key -> (value, tick), by_tick: tick -> key) are a hand-written persistent red-black tree over int keys, updated in place when unique (FBIP). Insert is the zipper insert of Koka's samples/basic/rbtree-fbip.kk; delete is Kahrs' (2001) algorithm; the evict takes by_tick's minimum. The loop is one tail-recursive function. The trees are generic, so the entries tree boxes its `value struct entry(value, tick)`, one small allocation per insert; packing value and tick into one int (a scratch test only) gained under 5% at bench, so the code keeps the generic tree rather than a second, monomorphic copy of it. Shape B (a mutable vector hash table and an index-linked list in local vars) is also allowed but is not what a fluent Koka programmer reaches for first.

ocaml/lru_cache.name: OCaml
ocaml/lru_cache.notes: Shape B: the generic Hashtbl from key to node, created with capacity slots, plus a circular doubly linked list of records with mutable prev/next fields around a sentinel node (no option boxes, so relinking allocates nothing); an evicted node is reused for the insert.

nim/lru_cache.name: Nim
nim/lru_cache.notes: Shape B: Table[int, int] from key to slot plus a seq of nodes linked by index; table and seq reserve capacity up front, as the SPEC allows.

ruby/lru_cache.name: Ruby
ruby/lru_cache.notes: Shape A: a plain Hash, which keeps insertion order. The lookup is Hash#delete, which returns the stored value on a hit (then re-inserted at the end); a miss evicts with Hash#shift.

cheby/ping_pong.name: Cheby
cheby/ping_pong.notes: fmt form checked by hand: `cheby fmt` does not exist before M5. Rerun `cheby fmt` once it lands.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/ping_pong.name: Gleam
gleam/ping_pong.notes: A is the process that runs main; B is process.spawn'ed and hands its ping subject to A over a setup subject once. Plain Subject(Int) messages, process.receive_forever, no join (B ends after its last reply).

rust-tokio/ping_pong.name: Rust (tokio)
rust-tokio/ping_pong.notes: #[tokio::main] (multi-thread runtime, default worker count). main runs through block_on on the main thread, so it spawns B and then A with tokio::spawn, awaits A's JoinHandle for the sum, then B's. Channels are tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(1): tokio's mpsc has no capacity 0.

zig/ping_pong.name: Zig
zig/ping_pong.notes: A is the main thread, B is started with io.concurrent on the std.Io.Threaded that main(init: std.process.Init) receives (default options, so B gets its own OS thread) and awaited through its Future. Channels are std.Io.Queue(i64) with a zero-length buffer (rendezvous), putOne and getOne.

cpp/ping_pong.name: C++
cpp/ping_pong.notes: Task A is the main thread, task B one std::thread, joined. Channels are one-slot channels built from std::mutex, two std::condition_variables and a std::optional slot (SPEC: capacity 0 and 1 do the same work here).

java/ping_pong.name: Java
java/ping_pong.notes: Virtual threads for A and B (Thread.ofVirtual().start); main joins A, reads its sum from a FutureTask, then joins B. Channels: SynchronousQueue<Long>, put/take.

typescript/ping_pong.name: TypeScript
typescript/ping_pong.notes: A is the main async function, B an async function whose promise is awaited after A's loop. Channels are a hand-written rendezvous Channel<T> on promises (queues of waiting receivers and senders, no value slot), per the SPEC; no setTimeout/setImmediate/queueMicrotask. Single-threaded event loop, so each handoff is a promise resolution (microtask), not a thread switch.

swift/ping_pong.name: Swift
swift/ping_pong.notes: Swift's async main (top-level code on the main actor) is task A; task B is a `Task { }` created from it, which inherits the main actor, so both run cooperatively on the main actor's executor (no Task.detached). Channels: one AsyncStream<Int> per direction (AsyncStream.makeStream, unbounded; the protocol keeps at most one message in flight). B is joined with `await b.value`. The bench run takes about 2.6-4 s, mostly sys time: every hop goes through the main actor's executor (the dispatch main queue), which wakes the kernel; next(isolation: #isolation) gives the same time, while isolating A and B to one custom actor or the global pool would take about 0.8 s but departs from the SPEC's layout.

csharp/ping_pong.name: C#
csharp/ping_pong.notes: Task A is the async top-level Main (no synchronization context, so after its first await it runs on the thread pool like B); task B is started with Task.Run and awaited at the end. Channels: Channel.CreateBounded<long>(new BoundedChannelOptions(0)), a true rendezvous since .NET 10, with FullMode = Wait, SingleReader and SingleWriter, one per direction, WriteAsync/ReadAsync (SPEC: capacity 0 where the primitive has it).

elixir/ping_pong.name: Elixir
elixir/ping_pong.notes: The main process is A; B is a plain `spawn`ed process. Messages are {:ping, i} and {:pong, x} sent with `send` and matched with `receive` (mailboxes, unbounded).

scala/ping_pong.name: Scala
scala/ping_pong.notes: Virtual threads for A and B (Thread.ofVirtual().start); main joins A, reads its sum from a FutureTask, then joins B. Channels: SynchronousQueue[Long], put/take.

clojure/ping_pong.name: Clojure
clojure/ping_pong.notes: Virtual threads for A and B ((.start (Thread/ofVirtual) f)); main joins A, reads its sum from a promise A delivers once at its end, then joins B. Channels: java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue, .put/.take (values boxed as Long).

clojure-coreasync/ping_pong.name: Clojure (core.async)
clojure-coreasync/ping_pong.notes: A and B are go blocks using the parking >! and <! on two unbuffered (chan)s; main takes A's result channel (the sum) and then B's with <!!, once each. Go blocks run as IOC state machines on core.async 1.9's default :mixed executor (an unbounded daemon cached thread pool, threads async-mixed-N; every parked handoff resumes via a Runnable submitted to it); no executor-factory or pool-size property set; no virtual threads. The library is AOT-compiled once by setup/clojure-coreasync.sh (CLJ_AOT_LIBS), so the build compiles only main.

koka/ping_pong.name: Koka
koka/ping_pong.notes: std/async ships with the installed Koka (precompiled, linked with libuv), so it counts as the standard library. A is a strand of `interleaved(a, b)` inside `async`, B the other strand; `interleaved` returns when both end (the join). Channels: std/async `channel()`, `emit` (never blocks, unbounded) and `receive`; the protocol keeps at most one message in flight. Strands are cooperatively scheduled on one thread.
koka/ping_pong.comparable_note: Koka: cooperative single-threaded std/async (no dynamic spawn); measured but not comparable, and left out of the geometric means

ocaml/ping_pong.name: OCaml
ocaml/ping_pong.notes: Thread.create/Thread.join (threads.posix) and synchronous Event channels, both in the OCaml distribution. OCaml int is 63-bit, wide enough for the sum.

ocaml-eio/ping_pong.name: OCaml (Eio)
ocaml-eio/ping_pong.notes: Eio_main.run (eio_posix backend on macOS, one domain). A is Eio's main fiber; B is Fiber.fork'ed into a Switch.run whose end joins it. Channels are Eio.Stream.create 0 (rendezvous), add/take. The posix scheduler polls for I/O (poll with a zero timeout) each time its run queue comes round, and with only two fibers alternating that is about once per handoff, so the row is dominated by that syscall and swings with machine load, like Python's asyncio.

ruby/ping_pong.name: Ruby
ruby/ping_pong.notes: OS threads under the GVL (Thread.new, join); SizedQueue.new(1), since SizedQueue has no capacity 0. A is the main thread.

cheby/spawn_many.name: Cheby
cheby/spawn_many.notes: fmt form checked by hand: `cheby fmt` does not exist before M5. Rerun `cheby fmt` once it lands. The run time at bench size (about 0.1 s) is an estimate with a large relative error. The run is sensitive to CPU oversubscription far more than Go or rust-tokio (about 0.12 s at load 10, 0.21 to 0.25 s at load 11 to 14 on 8 cores), so measure it only on an idle machine.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/spawn_many.name: Gleam
gleam/spawn_many.notes: main calls process.trap_exits(False) first, as Gleam's own main@@main:run wrapper does: the erl -eval process the run command uses traps exits, so each linked task's normal exit would otherwise queue an 'EXIT' message that every later receive scans past (quadratic; 19-35 s instead of ~0.2 s at bench).

rust-tokio/spawn_many.name: Rust (tokio)
rust-tokio/spawn_many.notes: #[tokio::main] (multi-thread runtime, default worker count). One tokio::spawn(async move { work(i) }) per index; each batch's JoinHandles are awaited in order and summed. The spawner is the #[tokio::main] future, which runs through block_on on the main OS thread, not on a worker: each spawn goes through the runtime's global inject queue, and each await of an unfinished handle parks the main thread (as the SPEC row describes).

zig/spawn_many.name: Zig
zig/spawn_many.notes: One std.Thread.spawn per index (default 16 MiB stack), joined with thread.join(); each thread writes only its own slot of a per-batch result slice, summed after the batch's joins.

cpp/spawn_many.name: C++
cpp/spawn_many.notes: One std::jthread (an OS thread) per task; each task writes only its own slot of a per-batch std::vector<std::int64_t>. The batch's std::vector<std::jthread> goes out of scope before the sum, so every thread is joined (jthread joins in its destructor) before the batch ends, as in the Rust, Zig, Odin and Nim rows. Replaces std::async(std::launch::async), whose future.get() in Apple libc++ returns before the detached thread exits and so did less join work than the other OS-thread rows (about 0.40 s vs 1.3 s at bench).

java/spawn_many.name: Java
java/spawn_many.notes: One Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() per batch (try-with-resources); one submit per index, Future.get() for each result.

typescript/spawn_many.name: TypeScript
typescript/spawn_many.notes: A task is an async function that first does `await Promise.resolve()` and then returns work(i); a batch is joined with `await Promise.all(batch)`. Node is single-threaded, so the tasks run on one thread as microtasks.

swift/spawn_many.name: Swift
swift/spawn_many.notes: One withTaskGroup(of: Int.self) per batch of 1,000; group.addTask { work(i) } per index, joined with `for await` over the group. Child tasks run on the default global concurrent executor (one thread per core).

csharp/spawn_many.name: C#
csharp/spawn_many.notes: Async top-level Main; each index is its own Task.Run(() => Work(index)) on the default thread pool, a batch of 1000 is joined with await Task.WhenAll and its results summed.

elixir/spawn_many.name: Elixir
elixir/spawn_many.notes: Task.async per index, Task.await_many(tasks, :infinity) per batch. main first sets Process.flag(:trap_exit, false): the `erl -eval` process that runs main traps exits, so each linked task's normal exit would otherwise stay in the mailbox and make the batch receives quadratic (84 s instead of 0.37 s at bench).

scala/spawn_many.name: Scala
scala/spawn_many.notes: One scala.concurrent.Future per index on ExecutionContext.global (the runtime's ForkJoinPool, default parallelism); each batch of 1000 joined with Await.result(Future.sequence(batch), Duration.Inf).

clojure/spawn_many.name: Clojure
clojure/spawn_many.notes: One (future (work i)) per index, a batch started with mapv so every future starts before the first deref; joined with deref, summed with reduce. Futures run on Clojure's agent send-off pool (cached platform threads owned by the runtime), as the SPEC table prescribes for Clojure, so this row measures pooled OS threads, not virtual threads; (shutdown-agents) at the end.

clojure-coreasync/spawn_many.name: Clojure (core.async)
clojure-coreasync/spawn_many.notes: One (go (work i)) per index, a batch started with mapv so every go block starts before the first take; joined with (<!! ch) on each go block's result channel, summed with reduce. Go blocks run as IOC state machines on core.async 1.9's default :mixed executor (an unbounded daemon cached thread pool, threads async-mixed-N; every parked handoff resumes via a Runnable submitted to it); no executor-factory or pool-size property set. The pool's threads are daemons, so no shutdown call is needed. The library is AOT-compiled once by setup/clojure-coreasync.sh (CLJ_AOT_LIBS).

koka/spawn_many.name: Koka
koka/spawn_many.notes: Per the SPEC's Koka row, the program writes its own cooperative scheduler as an effect handler (`effect tasks` with `spawn` and `join`): `spawn` queues a suspended task (a closure) in a FIFO and returns a handle (a ref cell for its result), `join` runs queued tasks until that handle's result is ready. Single-threaded, no stacks: a task here never blocks, so running it is a closure call. Not a runtime primitive, so not comparable with the other rows (std/async's `interleaved(list)` takes a fixed list and has no spawn handle). The batch's handles are built with an accumulator loop: `list.map` with an effectful function copies its TRMC context on every element (quadratic, 0.6 s instead of 0.02 s at bench).
koka/spawn_many.comparable_note: Koka: cooperative single-threaded std/async (no dynamic spawn); measured but not comparable, and left out of the geometric means

ocaml/spawn_many.name: OCaml
ocaml/spawn_many.notes: One systhread per task: Thread.create (threads.posix), a per-batch result array where task j writes slot j, Thread.join on each, then the array is summed. OCaml's 63-bit int holds every value exactly (x * 48271 < 2^47, sum < 2^53).

ocaml-eio/spawn_many.name: OCaml (Eio)
ocaml-eio/spawn_many.notes: Eio_main.run (one domain). One Switch.run per batch, one Fiber.fork_promise ~sw per index, then Promise.await_exn on each promise and the results summed. Eio starts a forked fiber at once, inside the fork call, so each task first does `Fiber.yield ()`: that suspends it on the run queue and returns to the spawner, and its work runs only after the spawn, when the first await suspends the spawner. A batch therefore holds all 1,000 of its tasks suspended before the first join, and the row measures deferred scheduling (queueing and resuming a suspended task), like TypeScript's `await Promise.resolve()` and the other rows. Without the yield each task would finish inside its fork and every await would find its promise already resolved; the yield roughly doubles the time (0.03 s to 0.065 s at n=100000).

ruby/spawn_many.name: Ruby
ruby/spawn_many.notes: One OS thread per index (Thread.new), joined with Thread#value; the GVL runs the work one thread at a time.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/prime_sieve.name: Gleam
gleam/prime_sieve.notes: Pull protocol: each stage creates its Subject(Next) request subject and Subject(Int) number subject once and hands the request subject to main over a setup subject. Shut down by option 1 (halt(0) after main with the stages blocked).

rust-tokio/prime_sieve.name: Rust (tokio)
rust-tokio/prime_sieve.notes: #[tokio::main] (multi-thread runtime, default worker count). The generator and every filter are tokio::spawn tasks; channels are tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(1), since tokio's mpsc has no capacity 0. Shutdown is option 2: main returns without awaiting its tasks, and dropping the runtime drops them all at once. With capacity 1 each stage can run one value ahead of its consumer before the shutdown, so this row does a few percent more filter work than the SPEC's counts (the Python row, also capacity 1 with option 2, measured +5.8% filter receives at bench). The driver loop (receive each prime, spawn its filter) is the #[tokio::main] future, which runs through block_on on the main OS thread, not on a worker, as the SPEC row allows: each prime crosses from a worker to the main thread, and each filter spawn goes through the runtime's global inject queue.

zig/prime_sieve.name: Zig
zig/prime_sieve.notes: Generator and filters are Io.Group.concurrent tasks on the std.Io.Threaded from main(init) (default options: unlimited concurrent_limit, one OS thread each, default 16 MiB stacks). Channels are heap-allocated std.Io.Queue(i64) with a zero-length buffer (rendezvous). Shutdown is option 1: flush stdout, then std.process.exit(0) without awaiting the group.

odin/prime_sieve.name: Odin
odin/prime_sieve.notes: core:thread + core:sync/chan unbuffered channels. Shutdown option 1: main returns with the stage threads still blocked, never joined; channels are never freed.

cpp/prime_sieve.name: C++
cpp/prime_sieve.notes: One detached std::thread per stage. Rendezvous channel from std::mutex and two std::condition_variables: send fills the slot, signals, then waits until a receiver has taken it (ticket counter); both sides signal after unlocking. Channels are std::shared_ptr held by the threads that use them; shutdown is option 1 (return from main with the threads blocked). The row (about 1.9 s at bench, about 3.4x Rust) pays for blocking condition variables: libc++ on macOS waits through pthread psynch and sleeps in the kernel at once, while Rust's std zero-capacity channel spins briefly before it parks. Notifying under the lock or with notify_one made no measurable difference.

python/prime_sieve.name: Python
python/prime_sieve.notes: One asyncio task per stage; channels are asyncio.Queue(maxsize=1), since Queue(maxsize=0) is unbounded. Shutdown is option 2: cancel() on every task, then asyncio.gather. With capacity 1 each stage can run one value ahead of its consumer, and that run-ahead happens before the cancel and inside the timed run: at bench a counting copy did 351,610 filter receives against the SPEC's 332,216 (+5.8%), with the generator reaching 6533 instead of 6133.

java/prime_sieve.name: Java
java/prime_sieve.notes: One virtual thread per stage, SynchronousQueue<Long> between stages; the main (platform) thread receives the primes. Shutdown option 1: virtual threads are daemons, so returning from main ends the JVM with the stages still blocked.

typescript/prime_sieve.name: TypeScript
typescript/prime_sieve.notes: Generator and filters are async functions on the hand-written rendezvous Channel<T> of ping_pong. Shut down with SPEC option 1: main prints and returns; the stages stay blocked on promises that never settle, which do not keep node alive (no process.exit).

swift/prime_sieve.name: Swift
swift/prime_sieve.notes: One unstructured `Task { }` per stage (generator and filters); the stage functions are nonisolated async, so they run on the global concurrent executor. Channels are a hand-written rendezvous `actor Channel` (queues of waiting receivers' and senders' CheckedContinuations, no value slot). Shutdown is option 1: the top-level code prints and returns, ending the process with the stages suspended.

csharp/prime_sieve.name: C#
csharp/prime_sieve.notes: Async top-level Main receives the primes; the generator and each filter are started with Task.Run. Channels: Channel.CreateBounded<long>(new BoundedChannelOptions(0)), a true rendezvous since .NET 10, with FullMode = Wait, SingleReader and SingleWriter (SPEC: capacity 0 where the primitive has it). Shutdown is SPEC option 2: one CancellationToken passed to every ReadAsync/WriteAsync is cancelled, then all tasks are awaited with Task.WhenAll (the OperationCanceledException is expected and caught).

elixir/prime_sieve.name: Elixir
elixir/prime_sieve.notes: Plain `spawn`, `send` and `receive` with the SPEC's pull protocol ({:next, from} / {:num, m}). Shut down by option 1: main returns and the run's halt(0) ends the blocked stages.

scala/prime_sieve.name: Scala
scala/prime_sieve.notes: One virtual thread per stage (Thread.ofVirtual().start), SynchronousQueue[Long] between stages; the main (platform) thread receives the primes, as in the Java row. Shutdown option 1: virtual threads are daemons, so returning from main ends the JVM with the stages still blocked.

clojure/prime_sieve.name: Clojure
clojure/prime_sieve.notes: One virtual thread per stage ((.start (Thread/ofVirtual) f)), java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue between stages (.put/.take, values boxed as Long); the main (platform) thread receives the primes. Shutdown option 1: virtual threads are daemons, so returning from -main ends the JVM with the stages still blocked.

clojure-coreasync/prime_sieve.name: Clojure (core.async)
clojure-coreasync/prime_sieve.notes: One go-loop per stage (generator and filters) with the parking >! and <! on unbuffered (chan)s; the JVM main thread receives the primes with <!!, as the main platform thread does in the clojure row. Go blocks run as IOC state machines on core.async 1.9's default :mixed executor (an unbounded daemon cached thread pool, threads async-mixed-N; every parked handoff resumes via a Runnable submitted to it); no executor-factory or pool-size property set. Shutdown option 1: that pool's threads are daemons, so returning from -main ends the JVM with the stages still parked. The library is AOT-compiled once by setup/clojure-coreasync.sh (CLJ_AOT_LIBS).

koka/prime_sieve.name: Koka
koka/prime_sieve.notes: The SPEC's Koka row says n/a ("no tasks or channels"), but std/async ships with the installed Koka (as in ping_pong), so this follows the SPEC with it. Strands of `firstof` inside `async`; channels are std/async `channel()`, `emit` and `receive`. `emit` never blocks, so the stages use the SPEC's pull protocol: each stage owns a request channel, and a request carries the requester's reply channel, created once. std/async has no dynamic spawn (`interleaved`/`firstof` take their strands up front), so each filter is started by a nested `firstof(filter, rest of the sieve)`, and shutdown is option 2: each `firstof` cancels its filter as the sieve returns. Every await is forwarded through all enclosing interleavings (std/async `emit-on-await`) and the root keeps its pending awaits in a list, so one handoff costs O(pipeline depth): about 70 s at bench (n = 800), against 0.6 s at n = 200. Single-threaded, cooperative.
koka/prime_sieve.comparable_note: Koka: cooperative single-threaded std/async (no dynamic spawn); measured but not comparable, and left out of the geometric means

ocaml/prime_sieve.name: OCaml
ocaml/prime_sieve.notes: One systhread per stage (Thread.create, threads.posix), synchronous Event channels (rendezvous) between stages; the main thread receives the primes. Shutdown is option 1: print, then exit 0 with the stages still blocked, never joined. Expected to be the slowest OS-thread row (5-7 s at bench; a 5-run median of 7.06 s, a single verify run 5.1 s): OCaml 5 systhreads of one domain share that domain's runtime lock, so every handoff between the 802 threads is also a runtime-lock handover. A Mutex + Condition channel of the C++ shape still took about 5 s, so Event adds about 1.4x and the lock is most of the cost.

ocaml-eio/prime_sieve.name: OCaml (Eio)
ocaml-eio/prime_sieve.notes: Eio_main.run (one domain). The generator and every filter are Fiber.fork_daemon fibers of one Switch.run; channels are Eio.Stream.create 0 (rendezvous). Shutdown is option 2: when the main fiber returns, the switch cancels every daemon at once and waits for them, then main prints.

ruby/prime_sieve.name: Ruby
ruby/prime_sieve.notes: OS threads under the GVL, n + 2 at once; SizedQueue.new(1) channels (no capacity 0). Shutdown option 1: the main thread ends and the process kills the blocked threads.

runtime_estimate.method: median run at bench size minus compile_estimate

gleam/compile_large.name: Gleam
gleam/compile_large.notes: One Gleam package `main`, src/m0000.gleam per module (custom types Item and Shape, pub base/entry). The langs/gleam.toml build/clean apply unchanged: the project is copied to {build}/proj and built with one cold `gleam build` (Gleam compiles modules in parallel by default); clean removes only build/dev/erlang/main, keeping gleam_stdlib compiled.

go/compile_large.name: Go
go/compile_large.notes: One package per module (m0000/m0000.go) in one module named main; module i imports "main/m<i-1>". Only Base and Entry are exported. Shape is a sealed interface (unexported isShape marker method, one per variant) with four structs, matched with a type switch. Built with plain `go build` (parallel by default); clean keeps only the std packages compiled in GOCACHE (langs/go.toml), so every generated package is compiled again. Serial by project shape: go build compiles one package at a time in dependency order, and the SPEC's import chain (package i imports only package i-1) leaves no two packages of the project ready at the same time, so the default package parallelism (-p) does nothing here; a review measured the M=200 build at 3.20 s with the default -p and 3.21 s with -p 1 (loaded machine). Read this row as serial because of the project's dependency chain, not because of the build command.

zig/compile_large.name: Zig
zig/compile_large.notes: src/main.zig plus src/m0000.zig..., each module @imports only the previous one; built with the plain langs/zig.toml command (zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast, --cache-dir {build}/zig-cache removed by clean). Integers are u64 (all values non-negative), Item is a struct, Shape a union(enum) matched with switch; only base and entry are pub. Output passes zig fmt --check. Zig compiles the whole program as one LLVM module, so the ReleaseFast build is effectively single-threaded (about 11 s wall at M = 200, user time about equal).

odin/compile_large.name: Odin
odin/compile_large.notes: One package per module (m0000/m0000.odin), module i imports "../m<i-1>" by relative path. Every item except base and entry is @(private) (package-private), matching the module-private reading of the Rust and Cheby references. Shape is a union of four structs matched with a type switch.

cpp/compile_large.name: C++
cpp/compile_large.notes: Generated Makefile, one object per module, built with `make -j$(sysctl -n hw.ncpu)` inside `sh -c` (hyperfine runs build without a shell). mNNNN.hpp declares base and entry in namespace mNNNN; everything else is in an anonymous namespace. Shape is a std::variant of four structs matched with std::visit and a plain per-module visitor struct with four operator() overloads (no template). No ccache, no PCH.

erlang/compile_large.name: Erlang
erlang/compile_large.notes: rebar3 project, built with `rebar3 compile` (parallel); erl_opts [deterministic, no_debug_info], the same flags as langs/erlang.toml's erlc +deterministic (rebar3 would otherwise add debug_info).

java/compile_large.name: Java
java/compile_large.notes: Flat default-package project: Main.java plus one final class M0000..M<M-1> per file, nested record Item and sealed interface Shape with four record variants matched by a switch pattern; base/entry package-private, the rest private. Main folds over a LongUnaryOperator[] of method references. One cold javac process over all files (javac has no parallel driver or daemon).

typescript/compile_large.name: TypeScript
typescript/compile_large.notes: One ES module per file (mNNNN.ts), module i does `import * as m<i-1>`. Item is an interface, Shape a discriminated union on `kind`, matched with switch; integer division is Math.trunc(a / k). The generated tsconfig loads the shared @types/node through typeRoots (a path relative from the generated project to build/typescript/node_modules/@types), like hello_world and every other TypeScript implementation, so compile-speed numbers share one declaration-input baseline even though the generated code uses no Node API. No incremental/composite; the langs/typescript.toml build and clean apply unchanged (one cold tsc 7 run, parallel by default). Generated code is Prettier-clean.

swift/compile_large.name: Swift
swift/compile_large.notes: One SwiftPM package `main` with one executable target: Sources/main/main.swift plus m0000.swift... per module, each wrapping its items in a caseless `enum M0000` namespace with a nested struct Item, a nested enum Shape with associated values (matched with switch) and static funcs; only base and entry are internal, the rest private. main folds with reduce over a literal [(Int) -> Int] of M0000.entry references. Built with `swift-build -c release --scratch-path {build}/swift --manifest-cache local`; clean removes every project-derived output in the scratch path and keeps only the SDK caches SwiftPM writes there (SDKStatCaches.noindex, SDKExplicitPrecompiledModules, ModuleCache.noindex: macOS SDK stat cache and SwiftShims/_SwiftConcurrencyShims .pcm, no project module), so the timed build does not re-precompile standard-library modules (about 0.8 s per build, measured at M=1: 2.1 s full clean against 1.35 s). Output passes swift-format lint.

csharp/compile_large.name: C#
csharp/compile_large.notes: One console project named main (the standard main.csproj), Program.cs with top-level statements plus one internal static class M0000..M<M-1> per file. Each module nests a sealed record Item and an abstract record Shape with four sealed derived records, matched by a switch expression with a throwing discard arm (C# has no exhaustiveness check over a record hierarchy). Base and Entry are internal, the rest private. Main folds over a Func<long, long>[] collection expression of method groups. Built with langs/csharp.toml's cold dotnet publish (no build servers, no shared compilation); csc compiles the files with its default parallelism.

elixir/compile_large.name: Elixir
elixir/compile_large.notes: One Mix project, app `main`, lib/m0000.ex per module (defmodule M0000 with a nested Item struct module, Shape as tagged tuples, defp for private functions). The langs/elixir.toml build/clean/run apply unchanged: one cold `mix compile` (MIX_ENV=prod, parallel by default, protocols consolidated); clean removes only _build/prod/lib/main.

scala/compile_large.name: Scala
scala/compile_large.notes: Flat default-package project: main.scala (top-level @main, folds over a List[Long => Long] of eta-expanded entry methods) plus one `object M0000`..`M<M-1>` per file with a private case class Item, a private enum Shape (four cases, matched with `match`) and 20 methods; base/entry public, the rest private. One cold scala-cli compile --server=false (scalac in a fresh JVM, no Bloop, no zinc state).

koka/compile_large.name: Koka
koka/compile_large.notes: One directory: main.kk and m0000.kk ... per module, `struct item` and `type shape`, built by the language's `build` (one `koka -O2` over main.kk, which compiles the imported modules and their C with parallel clang jobs). Names follow Koka's style (`make-item`, `step1`; `step-1` is not an identifier). Module i also sees module i-1's `base`, so step1 calls its own as `m<i>/base`. Bench (M = 200) does not build: Koka's generated C header for each module #includes the header of every module it imports, so the import chain m0199 -> m0198 -> ... -> m0000 nests 200 headers deep in m0199.c, and Apple clang stops at its fixed include-depth limit of 200 ("#include nested too deeply"; Apple clang 21 has no flag to raise it). M = 199 builds and prints the right checksum (388947, same as the Python reference), cold build about 22 s wall, 112 s CPU on a busy machine.

ocaml/compile_large.name: OCaml
ocaml/compile_large.notes: One dune project in one directory: dune-project, dune ((executable (name main))), main.ml and m0000.ml... per module, no .mli (so every item is visible, OCaml's default). Item is a record, Shape a variant matched with match; main folds over a literal list of M0000.entry values. The langs/ocaml.toml build/clean/run apply unchanged (dune --profile release, --cache disabled, parallel by default). The release profile compiles without -opaque, so ocamlopt of module i waits for the .cmx of module i-1 (cross-module inlining) and the import chain makes the native compile serial; a dev-profile build (-opaque) of M=200 took about 6.4 s against about 14.5 s in release on a loaded machine. The generated code builds warning-free in the dev profile.

nim/compile_large.name: Nim
nim/compile_large.notes: main.nim plus one module per index (m0000.nim ...) side by side; module i imports m<i-1>. Only base* and entry* are exported. Item is an object, Shape an object variant (case object on a ShapeKind enum) matched with case. Default langs/nim.toml build: nim c -d:release with the default --parallelBuild:0 (one clang per core); clean keeps the compiled std modules in the per-project nimcache (@p* files, after an untimed warm-up build when the project changed) and removes the project's own (@m* files, main.json, the executable), so Nim regenerates the C of every module and recompiles and links only the project's modules.

ruby/compile_large.name: Ruby
ruby/compile_large.notes: Timed as a full cold run: Ruby keeps no bytecode cache, so every run parses and compiles all modules. Data.define for Item and the Shape variants, case/in for area. Linter rule: the generated project is checked with `ruby -w` (no warnings); RuboCop is not part of the toolchain. The one-letter parameter `x` follows the SPEC's pseudo-code.
